content: Harm reduction and drug treatment services for people who inject drugs (PWID) have been successfully implemented in tuberculosis (TB) and sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics, as well as other healthcare services, with high rates of testing uptake. These approaches have been widely adopted in developed countries. Similar to HIV testing, hepatitis testing can be integrated into other health services and offered as part of a comprehensive care package. This can be done either routinely for all individuals accessing these services or targeted in specific clinical settings. Integrating screening into existing clinical services has been shown to be the most cost-effective method of testing, though it reaches fewer individuals. On the other hand, extending screening outside clinical settings is more expensive due to the additional costs of organizing events and utilizing volunteer time, but it reaches a larger population. Facility-based, provider-initiated HIV testing has been widely accepted in antenatal and TB clinic settings, as well as in drug treatment programs. These clinics can also serve as entry points for viral hepatitis testing, prevention, and care services, which are likely to be acceptable to patients attending these clinics. This approach helps normalize testing, reduces the potential embarrassment of clients requesting tests, and saves time for clients who are already accessing clinical services for other reasons. For hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing, determining the optimal strategic mix of approaches to increase diagnosis rates, particularly outside high-risk groups, depends on a country’s epidemic profile. A strategic framework is provided in Chapter 19 to guide countries in selecting testing approaches, while Chapter 17 offers specific examples of facilityand community-based service delivery models for viral hepatitis testing. There is a potential but uncertain risk of HBV reactivation and worsening liver disease during or after HCV clearance. Before initiating direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy, it is recommended to test for HBV infection (HBsAg, anti-HBc, and anti-HBs). If HBsAg is positive, HBV DNA testing should be performed to assess the need for concurrent HBV treatment, especially in populations and settings with a higher prevalence of HBV/HCV coinfection. Careful monitoring should continue after completing DAA therapy, including surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Testing strategies for chronic HBV infection and monitoring treatment response involve the use of serological assays, such as rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based immunoassays (e.g., enzyme immunoassay [EIA], chemiluminescence immunoassay [CLIA], or electrochemiluminescence assay [ECL]). These assays should meet minimum quality, safety, and performance standards, as defined by WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory review. Testing should be conducted in accordance with manufacturers’ instructions and, where possible, at sites enrolled in external quality assessment schemes. For diagnosing chronic HBV infection, a single serological assay to detect HBsAg is recommended before further evaluation for HBV DNA and liver disease staging. In settings with existing laboratory infrastructure, laboratory-based immunoassays are preferred. In areas with limited access to laboratory testing, RDTs are recommended to improve access and facilitate linkage to care and treatment. The choice between one-assay and two-assay serological testing strategies depends on the prevalence of HBsAg in the population and the diagnostic accuracy of the assays used. A one-assay strategy involves a single serological test, with reactive results reported as “compatible with HBsAg-positive” and non-reactive results as “HBsAg-negative.” A two-assay strategy adds a second test to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce false positives, and minimize inappropriate referrals to specialist services. The performance of RDTs and EIAs varies significantly. RDT sensitivity ranges from 50% to 100%, and specificity from 69% to 100%, depending on the brand and specimen type. EIAs generally demonstrate higher analytical sensitivity, with sensitivity ranging from 74% to 100% and specificity from 88% to 100%. Despite the variability, RDTs can be valuable in settings with limited laboratory infrastructure, such as remote areas or hard-to-reach populations. The WHO recommends standardized testing strategies to maximize the accuracy of HBsAg testing while minimizing costs and simplifying processes. The Guidelines Development Group emphasizes the need to expand testing to identify as many individuals as possible with chronic HBV infection who could benefit from antiviral treatment and other interventions. A simplified one-assay testing strategy using either EIA or RDTs is strongly recommended. In settings with laboratory infrastructure, EIAs are preferred due to their higher analytical sensitivity, automation capabilities, and cost-effectiveness when processing large volumes of tests. However, RDTs are recognized for their potential to scale up HBsAg testing in resource-limited settings, provided they meet minimum performance criteria. The benefits of increased access to testing with RDTs outweigh potential harms related to lower accuracy, especially with careful selection of high-quality RDTs. Further research is needed to simplify testing and care processes and integrate hepatitis services with other health services. This includes evaluating different service delivery models, such as communityor facility-based approaches, and conducting large-scale implementation studies in diverse epidemic settings and populations.
